sections.h2: Which Pine County offices deal with a property tax bill?
sections.html:
Two county offices share the work. The Assessor sets value and classification for roughly 32,000 parcels and answers at 320-591-1632. The Auditor-Treasurer computes the tax, mails statements, collects payment and handles delinquent accounts at 320-591-1670 from the courthouse at 635 Northridge Drive NW in Pine City. Both keep weekday hours from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The Assessor divides the county among appraisers by place. One covers Clover and Sandstone townships plus the cities of Pine City, Sandstone and Sturgeon Lake. Another takes Hinckley, Chengwatana and Pokegama townships and the city of Hinckley. A third works Barry, Crosby, Kettle River, Norman, Ogema and Pine City townships and the city of Rock Creek. Ask the front desk which appraiser has your parcel before you call about a value.

If you are selling a house, the Assessor's technicians also process homestead changes and electronic certificates of real estate value, while the Auditor-Treasurer gives payoff figures.

sections.h2: What kind of county is Pine County for a house seller?
sections.html:
Pine County sits on Minnesota's eastern edge, with the St. Croix River forming its boundary with Wisconsin. The county covers 1,435 square miles, of which 1,411 are land. The Kettle and Snake rivers cross it on their way to the St. Croix, and the terrain is low rolling hills that are partly wooded and partly farmed. Pine City, with Devil's Lake on its southeast edge, is the seat, and the county also holds Hinckley, Sandstone, Rock Creek, Askov, Willow River and eight other incorporated cities.

The county was created in 1856 and took its name from the abundant pine growth. An earlier version of the county was carved up in 1857 and the remaining territory was reorganized in 1872, when Pine City became the seat. Banning State Park, St. Croix State Park and part of Wild River State Park lie inside the boundary.

These Census Bureau QuickFacts figures give the context for pricing:

  • 30,472 residents on July 1, 2025, up 5.5% from the 2020 count
  • 17,905 housing units, 81.6% lived in by their owners
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home of $239,300 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median household income of $71,146 and a mean commute of 32.1 minutes
  • 213 building permits issued in 2025

The 2020 census counted nearly a third of the housing units as vacant, which reflects the cabins and seasonal places scattered through the lake and forest country.

sections.h2: What dates matter on the Pine County tax calendar?
sections.html:
The Assessor publishes a year-round list of state deadlines. The entries below are the ones a homeowner or seller most often needs, with the statute the county cites for each.

Selected Pine County property tax dates from the Assessor's dates and deadlines page
DateWhat happens
January 2Assessment date for real and personal property
March 31Last day for the Treasurer to mail tax statements
April 1 to May 31Window for local boards of appeal and equalization
April 30Last day to petition Minnesota Tax Court on value or class
May 15First-half payment due without penalty
June, after the second FridayCounty Board of Appeal and Equalization, with the exact day printed on the valuation notice
July 1Assessments become final for the year
August 15Last day to file the state property tax refund form M-1PR
October 15Second half due for non-farm property and special assessments
November 15Second half due on farm real property and manufactured homes
December 31Last day to establish homestead for the assessment year

The Auditor-Treasurer says statements go out in March and that a missing statement does not excuse a late payment. Mailed payments count as on time if the envelope is postmarked by the due date.

sections.h2: How do I challenge my Pine County value or classification?
sections.html:
Begin with the Assessor, and treat the spring valuation notice as the trigger. The sequence the county's calendar sets out looks like this:

  • Phone the Assessor at 320-591-1632 with your notice in hand and ask the appraiser for your area to review the value or class.
  • Attend the local board of appeal and equalization. It meets between April 1 and May 31, run by the township board or city council.
  • Take the case to the County Board of Appeal and Equalization in June. The notice gives the actual meeting date.
  • Petition Minnesota Tax Court by April 30 of the year the tax is payable if the boards do not settle it.

The county states that after July 1 no change in value or class can be made except where a statute allows it.

Bring evidence. A recent appraisal, a purchase contract or photographs of defects that the appraiser could not see from the road carry more weight than a general complaint about the increase.

sections.h2: How can I pay Pine County property tax, and what happens when I am late?
sections.html:
Checks and money orders go to Pine County Auditor-Treasurer, 635 Northridge Dr NW, Suite 230, Pine City, MN 55063. A drop box sits across from the main courthouse doors, and the office warns that cash must never go in it. You can also pay online or by phone at 1-800-272-9829 with jurisdiction code 3316, and in person with cash, check or money order. Card and e-check payments carry a service charge collected by the payment vendor, so read the current fee on the county payment page before you choose that route.

State law sets the late penalty for a first-half or second-half installment at 2% on homestead property and 4% on nonhomestead property the day after the deadline, with extra percentages added each month. After December 31 the county charges interest at 10% a year on what remains unpaid.

The county describes the delinquency path in steps:

  • Unpaid tax turns delinquent on January 1 of the next year.
  • Parcels still owing on February 15 go on a list filed with the court administrator, and the owner is mailed a letter.
  • The list is published twice in the newspaper, the first time by March 20.
  • On the second Monday in May, judgment is taken and the parcel is bid in for forfeiture. Owners generally have three years to redeem.

A confession of judgment lets an owner repay the delinquent total in a five-year or ten-year installment plan, as long as the current year's tax stays paid.

sections.h2: What should a Pine County seller know about taxes at closing?
sections.html:
The Treasurer's side of the courthouse collects current-year tax, deed tax and mortgage registry tax. For delinquent amounts or a payoff figure, call the Auditor's number, 320-591-1670. The county's own warning is that amounts shown online may be wrong where a payment plan exists, so ask for a written payoff before the closing date.

State law backs that up. A deed cannot be recorded unless the auditor has confirmed there is no delinquent tax, as section 272.12 directs. A sale above $3,000 also needs a certificate of value under section 272.115, and the assessor drops homestead status for the next year unless the buyer applies and qualifies. The state deed tax under section 287.21 is .0033 of net consideration on a sale over $3,000.

Manufactured homes follow their own track. The Auditor-Treasurer says a mobile home parcel cannot move into a new owner's name until the title is transferred, and a title transfer requires all current and delinquent personal property tax to be paid first.

sections.h2: Which Pine County tax breaks and refunds exist?
sections.html:
The county's FAQ points homeowners to the state refund on form M-1PR. You qualify for the regular refund if you owned and lived in the property on January 2 as your homestead. A special refund can apply when your tax rose more than 12 percent from the prior year. Forms come from the Department of Revenue, and the filing cutoff is August 15.

The Assessor's calendar lists several other deadlines worth noting: October 1 for the blind or permanently and totally disabled homestead classification, May 1 for Green Acres and managed forest applications, and December 31 for the disabled veteran market value exclusion. Owners who cannot pay should call the Auditor's office early, since staff can explain which option fits before forfeiture steps begin. Small overpayments of less than $5 are not refunded under a county board resolution.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a delinquent Pine County tax balance?
faqs.a: Call the Auditor-Treasurer at 320-591-1670. That office gives payoff amounts and sets up confession of judgment plans, and it warns that figures on the web can be wrong when an installment plan is in place.

faqs.q: When are Pine County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real property is due May 15 and October 15. Farm property and manufactured homes have a November 15 second half, and manufactured home first halves are due August 31. Check your statement for the exact amounts.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Pine County value after July 1?
faqs.a: Generally no. The county says assessments are final on July 1 and only changes allowed by statute can follow. The usual path runs through the local board, the June county board and Tax Court by April 30.

faqs.q: What if my Pine County tax statement never arrives?
faqs.a: Statements are mailed in March, and the county stresses that failing to receive one does not excuse a late payment. Look up the parcel on the county's online property site or ask the Auditor-Treasurer for a copy.

faqs.q: What refund can a Pine County homeowner claim from the state?
faqs.a: A homestead owner can file form M-1PR by August 15 for the property tax refund. A second, special refund can apply if the tax grew more than 12 percent. Get the form and instructions from the Minnesota Department of Revenue.
